description: Our team consists of six passionate members with diverse technical backgrounds, including DevOps, electrical engineering, and systems engineering. We share a strong passion for space exploration and technology, and we’re excited to combine our skills, creativity, and different perspectives to develop innovative solutions for the future of space exploration and astronaut health.
summary:
ARGUS is an autonomous AI crew medic that connects directly to the spacecraft’s computer. Astronauts don’t enter anything. Smart shirts, skin patches, sweat and microneedle sensors, and wearable ultrasound stream data continuously into the “Thousand Eyes”: dozens of indicators across 12 body systems, each judged against the astronaut’s own baseline. An interactive 3D Bio-Twin shows every organ’s status in green, yellow, or red.
How does it address the challenge?
ARGUS doesn’t just display data, it acts. If one astronaut develops a fever, ARGUS gives that person a spoken alert with what to do. If a problem affects the whole cabin, such as a CO₂ spike or an oxygen drop, ARGUS operates the ship’s systems itself, boosting scrubbers and airflow, and asks for confirmation only for critical actions. Its AI analyzes behavior, not just vitals: voice, facial cues, sleep, and daily cognitive games reveal stress, fatigue, and isolation. ARGUS also forecasts health three days ahead, briefs flight surgeons on Earth, and builds each astronaut a personal recovery plan for the return home.

Why is it important?
On the way to Mars, Earth can be 20 minutes away. ARGUS runs fully offline and gives every crew its own medical team.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
ARGUS is an autonomous AI crew medic for deep-space missions. Astronauts wear smart shirts, skin patches, sweat and microneedle sensors, and wearable ultrasound, so health data flows in continuously with nothing to type. The “Thousand Eyes” engine tracks dozens of indicators across 12 body systems. It compares each reading to the astronaut’s own baseline, adjusts it for the mission environment (ISS, Moon, Mars, or transit), and uses statistical drift detection to catch changes early. A deterministic triage engine rates each indicator green, yellow, or red and calculates a Crew Readiness Score, which an interactive 3D Bio-Twin displays organ by organ.

ARGUS then acts:

  • Individual alerts: if one astronaut shows a dangerous value, ARGUS gives that person a spoken alert with clear steps.
  • Spacecraft control: if a problem affects the whole cabin, such as a CO₂ spike or an oxygen drop, ARGUS connects to the ship’s systems and fixes it itself, for example by boosting scrubbers and airflow. Safe actions run automatically and can be undone, significant ones need crew confirmation, and life-support shutdowns are never automated.
  • Behavioral analysis: the AI combines voice, facial cues, mood, sleep, and daily NASA Cognition-based games to detect stress, fatigue, and isolation, then suggests countermeasures.
  • Earth link: ARGUS queues delay-tolerant reports to flight surgeons, forecasts health three days ahead, and builds a 45-day recovery plan for the return to Earth.

Benefits
ARGUS detects problems before symptoms appear, reduces the crew’s workload, gives plain-language guidance to non-physicians, and keeps the crew in control. It works fully offline.

Intended impact
ARGUS aims to make crews medically self-sufficient on missions where help from Earth is up to 20 minutes away. By forecasting each astronaut’s health three days ahead, it lets crews prevent problems instead of reacting to emergencies, turning every crew into its own medical team.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript (frontend, backend, and shared logic) and Python (data analysis notebooks).
  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (React Three Fiber) for the 3D Bio-Twin, and Recharts for trends.
  • Backend: Hono on Node.js, Zod for validation, and PostgreSQL with pgvector (Azure, or embedded PGlite for offline use), managed with Drizzle ORM.
  • AI:
    • A multi-provider chain: local models via Ollama or LM Studio, plus Gemini, Groq, and OpenRouter.
    • A RAG knowledge base of verified NASA protocols that the AI cites before giving procedures.
    • Gemini Live for real-time voice, and offline speech-to-text and text-to-speech (Transformers.js, Kokoro).
    • On-device vision with MediaPipe and face-api for Face ID and facial cues.
  • Data: NASA OSDR (Inspiration4 blood counts) and radiation datasets, with 99 cited sources from NASA HRP and CSA.
  • Hardware: built to integrate with wearable sensors such as the Bio-Monitor smart shirt, sweat and microneedle patches, and wearable ultrasound, and to connect with the spacecraft’s environmental control systems.

What makes it creative

  • ARGUS works like a smart-home assistant for the spacecraft: it sees, understands, and acts, rather than just showing dashboards.
  • It doesn’t wait for something to go wrong. ARGUS forecasts each astronaut’s health three days ahead, warning the crew about tomorrow’s problems while there’s still time to prevent them.
  • It distinguishes one sick astronaut from a sick cabin and responds to each differently.
  • Its AI decides how to respond based on distance from Earth, moving from live cloud AI to fully on-board models.
  • It includes human touches, such as a photobooth that emails photos to family with a real light-time delay.
  • when the crew lands, ARGUS greets them by voice and opens each astronaut’s personal recovery plan.

Factors we considered

  • Safety: clinical triage is computed in deterministic code, and the AI can raise a concern but never lower it.
  • Communication delay and blackouts: everything works offline.
  • Evidence: every threshold is grounded in NASA HRP sources.
  • Privacy: face recognition runs on the device, and astronauts see only their own data.
  • Usability: plain language, voice interaction, English red-flag detector.
  • Psychological wellbeing and post-mission recovery.
